questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073335/assets/2fff2eab1f5670dfcd3351dcbb9be1b3110e6ebdcd452cf4c5a273611d454c8b.png)

Consider the vector field $F=⟨1,\,0,\,x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of the solid onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=0$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=-\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper plane ${S}_{1}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is upward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨1,0,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower hemisphere ${S}_{2}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=\frac{y}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=1,\,Q=0,\,R=x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂h}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-1\cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-0\cdot \frac{y}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $F=⟨-y,\,z,\,0⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of the solid onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=0$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-4$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper plane ${S}_{1}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is upward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨-y,z,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}0\,\text{d}A \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower cone ${S}_{2}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-4)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-4)=\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=-y,\,Q=z=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-4,\,R=0.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂h}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-(-y)\cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-4)\cdot \frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-y+\frac{4y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y-\frac{xy+4y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & =0+{∬}_{D}y-\frac{xy+4y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y-\frac{xy+4y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $F=⟨{z}^{2},\,0,\,y⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So, 

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=0$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper hemisphere ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=-\frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P={z}^{2}=4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,Q=0,\,R=y.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot (-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})-0\cdot (-\frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})+y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}+y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,-1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨{z}^{2},0,y⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}+y\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}-y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073335/assets/0e374f18d8b87de2fddd9a2127ee84709746c7c1b75083441afcc7b6c79402fb.png)

Consider the vector field $F=⟨-z,\,0,\,x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So, 

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=0$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper paraboloid ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=-z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-5,\,Q=0,\,R=x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-5)\cdot (-2x)-0\cdot (-2y)+x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-10x+x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-9x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,-1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨-z,0,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-9x)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}-x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-10x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

$$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$

$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=-y,\,Q=0,\,R=x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-(-y)\cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-(0)\cdot \frac{y}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(\frac{xy}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-2)=0 \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-2)=2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P={z}^{2}={({y}^{2}-2)}^{2},\,Q=0,\,R=-x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂h}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-{({y}^{2}-2)}^{2}\cdot (0)+0\cdot (2y)+(-x))\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-x)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F=⟨1,\,0,\,-x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that encloses the finite region between the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ and the plane $z=1+x.$ Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=1+x$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper plane ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1+x)=1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1+x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=1,\,Q=0,\,R=-x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1\cdot 1-0\cdot 0+(-x))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider lower paraboloid ${S}_{2}.$ 

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=1,\,Q=0,\,R=-x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-1\cdot 2x-0\cdot 2y+(-x))\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-2x-x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1-x)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}3x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x-1\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F=⟨0,\,z,\,y⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that encloses the finite region between the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ and the hemisphere $z=\sqrt{5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}.$ Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=\sqrt{5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper hemisphere ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=-\frac{y}{\sqrt{5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=0,\,Q=z=\sqrt{5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}},\,R=y.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂h}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-0\cdot (-\frac{x}{\sqrt{5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})-\sqrt{5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{y}{\sqrt{5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(0+y+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower paraboloid ${S}_{2}.$ 

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=0,\,Q=z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2},\,R=y.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-0\cdot (2x)-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot (2y)+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(0-2y{x}^{2}-2{y}^{3}+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2y{x}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2y\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}2y{x}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2y{x}^{2}+2{y}^{3}+y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073335/assets/263853df5f080da778a34caacea945119099326f0ba27806d851f793416e9f92.png)

 

Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F} = \langle 0, \, x, \, -z^2 \rangle$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of the solid onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
\displaystyle
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} 
=
\iint\limits_D \,\bbox[3pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAA}} \: \textrm{d}A.
$$

Determine the missing expression.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface $S_1: z = g(x,y) = 0$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface $S_2: z = h(x,y) = -\sqrt{4 - x^2 - y^2}$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper plane $S_1.$ 

Since the positive orientation is upward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n} = \langle 0,0,1 \rangle.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨0,x,-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}0\,\text{d}A \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower hemisphere $S_2.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z = h(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=\frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $\mathbf{F}=\langle P, \, Q, \, R \rangle,$ then

$$
P = 0, \qquad
Q = x, \qquad
R = -z^2 = x^2 + y^2 - 4.
$$

 
As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂h}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-0\cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-x\cdot \frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{xy}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{xy}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F} = \langle x, \, y, \, 0 \rangle$ and the closed surface $S$ that encloses the finite region between the parabolic cylinder $z=1-x^2$ and the paraboloid $z=x^2+y^2.$ Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
\displaystyle
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} 
=
\iint\limits_D \,\bbox[3pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAA}} \: \textrm{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface $S_1: z=g(x,y)=1-x^2$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface $S_2: z=h(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper parabolic cylinder $S_1.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-{x}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1-{x}^{2})=0\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $\mathbf{F}=\langle P, \, Q, \, R \rangle,$ then

$$
P = x, \qquad
Q = y, \qquad
R = 0.
$$

 
As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-x\cdot (-2x)-y\cdot (0)+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower paraboloid $S_2.$ 

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $\mathbf{F}=\langle P, \, Q, \, R \rangle,$ then

$$
P = x, \qquad
Q = y , \qquad
R = 0.
$$

 
As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂h}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-x\cdot (2x)-y\cdot (2y)+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$
